Suppose it’s 2016. Meridian Pictures, a mid-sized film studio, is preparing its Strategy & Slate Planning review for the coming development cycle. To support this, Meridian has engaged Monash University’s Department of Econometrics and Business Statistics for a short consulting project - the engagement was arranged through Dr Minh Huynh, who is acting as the project’s methodological sign-off authority on Monash’s side. You are working as a team of four within this engagement, reporting to Meridian’s Head of Production and Finance team.

You have been provided with a dataset, see the Data tab, containing a historical sample of theatrically released films up to the end of 2016, compiled from The Movie Database (TMDB) together with cast and crew records for each film. The Head of Production and the studio’s Finance team understand basic descriptive statistics but are not familiar with statistical modelling or inference. They are happy for you to use whatever techniques are appropriate, provided you can explain the results to them in plain language.

CautionImportant

As a condition of the engagement, Dr Huynh has asked that the team only use methods the Department has formally trained you on and is prepared to stand behind professionally - this is standard practice for a University-backed consulting engagement, where the Department’s name is attached to whatever methodology goes out the door. In practice, that means every technique in your final report should be one you’ve covered in your coursework; if you find yourself reaching for something you’ve only encountered outside your training, treat that as a signal to look for the appropriate covered technique instead, not as a way to sidestep it.

The data provided, is a historical sample of theatrically released films with reported budgets, box office revenue, genre, franchise status, and cast/crew information. Because these are self-reported industry figures rather than audited accounts, some fields contain missing-data placeholders (most commonly budget or revenue recorded as 0, and a small number of implausibly tiny budget values) — identifying and handling these appropriately is part of the task, not a data-cleaning step you should skip over.


The key variables are described below:

Film Dataset: Variable Dictionary
Definitions and guidance for key variables
Variable Description
budget Reported production budget (USD). Values of 0 and implausibly small values (e.g., below $10,000) are missing-data placeholders, not real budgets.
revenue Reported worldwide box-office revenue (USD). Zero indicates missing data, not a genuine zero-revenue release.
profit Revenue minus budget.
roi Revenue divided by budget. Undefined (missing) where budget is 0.
runtime Length of the film, in minutes.
primary_genre The first-listed genre for the film. A film may have several genres; see genre_list.
genre_list Full list of genres assigned to the film.
franchise_status Whether the film is classified as “Franchise” or “Original”. Franchise films are identified as sequels or follow-on films using title patterns or keyword tags.
primary_company / primary_country Lead production company and country.
vote_average / vote_count / popularity Audience and critical-reception metrics from the platform. These are not the same as box-office performance.
director / lead_actor / cast_size / crew_size Extracted from cast and crew records: credited director, top-billed actor, size of the credited cast, and total crew count.
n_directors / n_producers / n_writers Counts of credited people in each of these crew roles.
n_visual_effects_crew / n_camera_crew / n_sound_crew Department headcounts from the crew list—a proxy for production complexity independent of the reported budget figure.
release_year / release_month Parsed from the film’s release date.

Meridian’s distribution partner has also confirmed the number of release slots contracted for the coming financial year (reminder: pretend it’s 2016, so the next FY would be 2017) in each of the five genres the studio is focused on:

  • Action: 8
  • Comedy: 10
  • Drama: 12
  • Horror: 6
  • Animation: 4

Slate Health Check (20 marks)

Before any decisions are made, the studio wants a high-level overview of the financial health and composition of its historical slate.

Required analyses and components:

  1. Provide a summary table of the following variables: production budget, return on investment (ROI), and franchise status (Franchise/Original).
  2. Create appropriate visualisations of those variables from part a, showing their overall distribution and also how they compare across genres.
  3. Investigate whether the composition of the slate has shifted over time (e.g. by release year): budgets, ROI, and/or the franchise/original mix, and comment on any trend the Head of Production should be aware of.
  4. Write a brief summary (3 - 4 paragraphs max) for the Head of Production, including the key details that can be observed about these variables. Note any data quality issues (e.g. missing or placeholder values) you had to address first.

Franchise vs. Original: Investment Strategy (20 marks)

As part of a creative-diversity push, Meridian’s leadership wants to greenlight more original (non-franchise) projects. They are concerned that the current Original slate consists mostly of small, low-budget projects, while the Franchise slate absorbs much larger budgets and generates the majority of studio revenue.

Required analyses and components:

  1. Use an appropriate visualisation to compare the full budget distributions of the Franchise and Original groups across the whole dataset. Describe any key similarities and differences.
  2. Calculate a 95% interval estimate for the difference in median budget between the two groups.
  3. Discuss whether your findings support leadership’s concern.
  4. Based on your findings, what advice would you give Meridian about its investment strategy over the next decade? How should the studio balance franchise and original projects?

Modelling Budgets & Downside Risk (20 marks)

Meridian’s Finance team needs two related but separate things for planning purposes.

  • First, a realistic probability model for production budgets - benchmarked against Universal Pictures, one of Meridian’s direct competitors, since Finance wants a credible external reference point.
  • Second, a downside-risk figure for the Action genre, Meridian’s own most capital-intensive genre, defined as the 25th percentile of the ROI distribution (the return multiple below which the worst quarter of films fall).

Required analyses and components:

  1. Fit a normal distribution to the budgets of Universal Pictures films (as primary_company), and at least one alternative distribution family (e.g. gamma, log-normal, or Weibull). Use an appropriate diagnostic (e.g. a Q-Q plot) and AIC to decide which is the more realistic model, and explain why.
  2. Now consider all studios, instead of just Universal Pictures. Finance wants to know how badly a film in the worst quarter of the Action genre tends to perform. Specifically, calculate an appropriate 95% interval estimate for the 25th percentile of ROI for films in the Action genre, using at least two different estimation methods.
  3. Compare the results of your percentile estimators. Do they agree, and if not, why might that be, considering the assumptions of each method and the characteristics of the Action-genre data?
  4. Write a brief summary for the Finance team covering both results: which budget distribution you’d recommend for their simulator (based on the Universal Pictures analysis), and what downside-risk figure they should plan around for the Action slate.

Building a Greenlight Risk Model (20 marks)

So far you have assessed risk in aggregate: across a whole genre, or across broad slate segments like Franchise vs. Original. The Head of Production wants something more targeted: a model that flags whether an individual pitch is likely to flop (fail to recoup its budget, i.e. ROI < 1) using only information that is known before the film is greenlit, e.g. its proposed genre, franchise status, budget, and planned production scale.

Required analyses and components:

  1. Define “flop” as a binary outcome (ROI < 1), and briefly justify why logistic regression (rather than a linear or Poisson model) is the appropriate choice for this kind of outcome.
  2. Fit both a frequentist logistic regression and a Bayesian logistic regression, with weakly informative priors on the log-odds scale) for flop probability, using at least genre, franchise status, budget (or log budget), and one crew-based variable (e.g. cast size) as predictors. Report and interpret the coefficients as odds ratios, compare the frequentist confidence intervals to the Bayesian credible intervals for at least two coefficients, and report at least one posterior probability statement.
  3. Assess model fit using a confusion matrix and the associated accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and precision at an appropriate classification threshold. Justify your choice of threshold given how rare flops are in the data.
  4. Use your model to estimate the flop probability (with uncertainty) for two or three hypothetical pitches of your choosing, give a greenlight recommendation for each, and write a brief, non-technical summary for the Head of Production on what the model can and can’t be trusted to tell them.

There is a total of 100 marks available for this assignment. This is split into the following broad areas.

Technical Content (80 marks)

Up to 80 marks are available for correctness and completeness of your responses to the four Tasks in the assignment (the specific mark allocations for each Task are given below).

Communication & presentation (10 marks)

Up to 10 marks are available for communication and presentation quality, as follows:

  • Structure & cohesion [5 marks]. Whether the document is structured in a clear manner, is easy to navigate, and has a consistent tone and notation.

  • Professional presentation [5 marks]. Whether the document is presented neatly and at a standard that would be deemed acceptable to give to a client or manager. Plots should use a clean design, with appropriate colour scales, and clear, descriptive labels. Tables should also be clean and use appropriate headings. Numerical results should be reported to an appropriate number of significant figures.

Reproducibility (5 marks)

Up to 5 marks will be awarded for submitting a correct set of files (as per the above instructions) and whether the submitted Quarto file compiles as submitted without error.

Collaboration (5 marks)

The remaining 5 marks will be awarded based on the quality of your collaboration and documentation of it (i.e. the Appendix), as follows:

  • Project plan & timeline. This must include a meeting schedule, an allocation of duties for each group member, and a plan for how each member’s work will be merged into the final submission. Each piece of work should have at least one nominated “reviewer” within the group, to ensure quality and cohesion of the final submission.

  • Statement of contributions. An appendix in the final report detailing who did what. It must include a “cross-review table” showing which team members verified each section of your code/analysis.

We expect each group member to contribute equally to each group, and to complete the peer evaluation survey. Marks may be deducted if any instructions are not followed, and responses from the peer evaluation survey may be used to adjust your individual mark. If you provide less than full marks for a team member on the peer review survey, you will need to provide a reason why.
